behavior_items: The reproducer defines a minimal coroutine return type `Coroutine` with the required nested `promise_type` and a `std::coroutine_handle<promise_type>` used to resume the coroutine manually from `main`.

The coroutine body is the lambda `[]() -> Coroutine { co_return; }`, so the presence of `co_return` makes the lambda a coroutine and causes the compiler to synthesize the standard coroutine transformation around an otherwise trivial body.

`promise_type::get_return_object()` constructs the externally visible `Coroutine` object from `handler_type::from_promise(*this)`, allowing the caller to store the coroutine handle and later call `resume()` on it.
`promise_type::initial_suspend()` returns a custom awaiter type `initial_suspend_awaiter`, so the coroutine always performs an initial `co_await` before executing the user body.
The custom awaiter reports `await_ready() == false`, which forces suspension logic to be generated rather than allowing the coroutine to continue immediately.
`await_suspend(handler_type)` is a no-op returning `void`, meaning the coroutine suspends at the initial suspend point and control returns to the caller after coroutine creation.

Because of that initial suspension, the lambda call in `main` creates the coroutine frame and returns a `Coroutine` object whose handle refers to a suspended coroutine that has not yet executed the `co_return` body.

The explicit `coro.handler.resume();` in `main` resumes execution from the initial suspend point, causing the coroutine runtime to complete the `co_await promise.initial_suspend()` protocol and then continue into the trivial body.

The key trigger is `initial_suspend_awaiter::await_resume()`, whose return type is a class type (`using await_resume_return_object = struct{};`). The returned object is unused because `co_await promise.initial_suspend();` appears as a statement expression in the coroutine prologue.

Semantically, the initial suspend expression is generated by the compiler as part of coroutine lowering; its result is discarded, so the compiler should still correctly materialize, ignore, and destroy any temporary object produced by `await_resume()` when that return type is non-void and non-reference.

The bug report notes that changing `await_resume()` to return `int` avoids the failure, showing that GCC handles discarded scalar results correctly but miscompiles the case where the discarded result is a class prvalue.

This strongly suggests the exercised compiler path is the coroutine lowering for the synthetic initial-suspend `co_await`, specifically the code that builds or cleans up the discarded `await_resume()` result object when its type requires class-object semantics.

The reproducer is intentionally minimal: the awaiter has explicit constructor/destructor, `await_suspend` does nothing, and the coroutine body immediately `co_return`s, so almost all observable complexity comes from compiler-generated coroutine machinery rather than user code.

The quoted standard transformation is central to the reproducer: it emphasizes that the coroutine behaves as if it begins with `co_await promise.initial_suspend();` inside the synthesized prologue, before the user body and before exception handling falls through to `unhandled_exception()`.

Since the initial await's result is not bound to any variable and not otherwise consumed, the compiler must treat it as a discarded-value expression. The reproducer checks whether GCC can lower that discarded `co_await` correctly when `await_resume()` yields a class object.

The reported failure mode is a compiler segmentation fault, not a runtime crash of the generated program. So the bug is in GCC's internal compilation of the coroutine transformation rather than in execution of the source program.

The same source structure also distinguishes between front-end semantic correctness and backend/lowering robustness: the program is valid C++ coroutine code, and the crash indicates GCC hits an internal error while processing a legal but less common case.

The reproducer exercises a narrow corner case: class-valued `await_resume()` on the awaiter returned by `promise.initial_suspend()`, with the result immediately discarded in the compiler-synthesized coroutine prologue. That combination is what isolates the bug.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: The failure pattern is tightly localized to GCC's coroutine lowering for the compiler-synthesized `co_await promise.initial_suspend()` expression. Wrap a SAVE_EXPR around EXPR, if appropriate. Do this to any expression which may be used in more than one place, but must be evaluated only once. Normally, expand_expr would reevaluate the expression each time. Calling save_expr produces something that is evaluated and recorded the first time expand_expr is called on it. Subsequent calls to expand_expr just reuse the recorded value. The call to expand_expr that generates code that actually computes the value is the first call *at compile time*. Subsequent calls at compile time* generate code to use the saved value. This produces correct result provided that *at run time* control always flows through the insns made by the first expand_expr before reaching the other places where the save_expr was evaluated. You, the caller of save_expr, must make sure this is so. Constants, and certain read-only nodes, are returned with no SAVE_EXPR because that is safe. Expressions containing placeholders are not touched; see tree.def for an explanation of what these are used for.

Subroutine of stabilize_reference; this is called for subtrees of references. Any expression with side-effects must be put in a SAVE_EXPR to ensure that it is only evaluated once. We don't put SAVE_EXPR nodes around everything, because assigning very simple expressions to temporaries causes us to miss good opportunities for optimizations. Among other things, the opportunity to fold in the addition of a constant into an addressing mode often gets lost, e.g. "y[i+1] += x;". In general, we take the approach that we should not make an assignment unless we are forced into it - i.e., that any non-side effect operator should be allowed, and that cse should take care of coalescing multiple utterances of the same expression should that prove fruitful.

gcc/stmt.cc.signature: static void emit_case_dispatch_table (tree index_expr, tree index_type, auto_vec<simple_case_node> &case_list, rtx default_label, edge default_edge, tree minval, tree maxval, tree range, basic_block stmt_bb)
gcc/stmt.cc.summary: Generate a dispatch tabler, switching on INDEX_EXPR and jumping to one of the labels in CASE_LIST or to the DEFAULT_LABEL. MINVAL, MAXVAL, and RANGE are the extrema and range of the case labels in CASE_LIST. STMT_BB is the basic block containing the statement. First, a jump insn is emitted. First we try "casesi". If that fails, try "tablejump". A target *must* have one of them (or both). Then, a table with the target labels is emitted. The process is unaware of the CFG. The caller has to fix up the CFG itself. This is done in cfgexpand.cc.

gcc/stmt.cc.signature: void expand_sjlj_dispatch_table (rtx dispatch_index, vec<tree> dispatch_table)
gcc/stmt.cc.summary: Expand the dispatch to a short decrement chain if there are few cases to dispatch to. Likewise if neither casesi nor tablejump is available, or if flag_jump_tables is set. Otherwise, expand as a casesi or a tablejump. The index mode is always the mode of integer_type_node. Trap if no case matches the index. DISPATCH_INDEX is the index expression to switch on. It should be a memory or register operand. DISPATCH_TABLE is a set of case labels. The set should be sorted in ascending order, be contiguous, starting with value 0, and contain only single-valued case labels.
